In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the chloroplasts of higher plants are capable of catalyzing the complete carbon reduction sequence, from carbon dioxide to carbohydrate, in the presence of light, ferredoxin, and a catalytic amount of ATP and N.ADP. The

the lag in photosynthesis is due to the fact that in the intact chloroplast, as well as in the reconstituted one, a certain concentration of ATP is needed before the full photosynthetic capacity can be reached.

the reconstituted systems described here are not only capable of photosynthesis at rates comparable to those of whole chloroplasts but also exhibit the same autocatalytic behavior as do whole chloroplasts and whole plants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the reconstitution of photosynthetic CO(2) assimilation from isolated stromal components is feasible.

the chloroplast is a highly organized, self-contained system capable of catalyzing a variety of metabolic reactions and of maintaining the necessary concentrations of intermediates to sustain these reactions at rates that are not readily achieved in the absence of the intact chloroplast.

the reconstituted systems, like intact chloroplasts and whole plants, are capable of autocatalytic CO(2) fixation and that the mechanism of autocatalysis in all three systems appears to involve a positive feedback loop between CO(2) assimilation and ATP synthesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the reconstituted systems can provide an excellent model for studies of the mechanisms and regulation of the carbon cycle in chloroplasts and that, in addition to the ATP and NADPH required for CO(2) fixation, the system also requires the presence of a small amount of carbon cycle intermediate(s) for full expression of its photosynthetic capacity.
the chloroplast is a highly integrated organelle in which the activities of many enzymes and protein components are tightly coupled to the activities of the ATP and NAD(P)H pools.
the lag in the rate of CO(2) fixation is a consequence of the slow accumulation of the carbon cycle intermediates, and is not caused by a slow rate of photosynthetic electron transport.
